  • *Malignant ascites*: Usually exudative, often associated with weight loss, anorexia, or palpable masses — none reported; also, dyspnea would be less prominent unless there’s pleural involvement or massive volume overload — but again, edema would be expected with hypoalbuminemia or capillary leak.  
  • *Nephrotic syndrome*: Requires severe hypoalbuminemia (<2.5 g/dL) to cause ascites without edema — extremely rare; and would show heavy proteinuria, hyperlipidemia — none assessed yet, but absence of edema contradicts typical physiology.

Crucially, the *most discriminating pending test is the echocardiogram* — which will directly assess pericardial thickness, calcification, septal bounce, exaggerated respiratory variation in mitral/tricuspid inflow, and IVC plethora — all hallmarks of constriction. But even pre-echo, the clinical gestalt — subacute onset, ascites-dominant fluid retention, dyspnea without pulmonary congestion signs, and *lack of peripheral edema* — points most specifically to constrictive pericarditis.
